https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/00.title: Anatomy- and Site-Guided 3D Patch Diffusion for Robust MRI Harmonization
https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/00.description: Abstract Pooling multi-site T1-weighted MRI increases power but introduces scanner-driven variability that can bias analyses. We propose a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for MRI harmonization that preserves fine anatomical details while aligning image contrast across sites. Our method constructs site-invariant anatomical maps using gradient and high-frequency features, which guide patch-wise diffusion synthesis together with learnable site embeddings. Processing overlapping high-resolution patches avoids latent-decoder blurring and reduces memory requirements, enabling faithful preservation of fine anatomical detail. To further enhance anatomical fidelity, we employ manifold-constrained classifier-free guidance, stabilizing diffusion sampling while maintaining subject-specific structures. We evaluate our framework on a multi-site traveling-subject dataset and a clinically acquired pathological cohort, comparing against state-of-the-art harmonization methods. Results show that our approach effectively reduces site-related intensity variability, preserves anatomical and tissue-specific information, and maintains clinically relevant brain–cognition associations. These findings demonstrate that patch-based, anatomy-guided diffusion harmonization provides a robust, high-fidelity solution for multi-site MRI, with clear practical benefits for clinical datasets and downstream analyses. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/barna-hache/PatchLevelDiffusionMRIHarmonization. Derivation of anatomical representations that are supposedly site-invariant is a critical step in the proposed framework for structural MRI harmonization. As such, greater detail should be provided on how Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) tests in Ablation Study 2 demonstrate site-invariance of the anatomical conditioning map. What specific distribution pairs were MMDs calculated between? How was MMD averaged per site when MMDs were calculated on inter-site discrepancies? STGAN and HACA3 outperform the proposed framework in matched-subject harmonization performance (SSIM, WD, PCC). STGAN, HACA3, and basic preprocessing outperform the proposed framework in mixed-effects modeling of brain tissue volumes, albeit not consistently. For what tasks or under what circumstances would the authors recommend the proposed framework be utilized over STGAN or HACA3? While the curated training and clinical datasets are robust in spanning multiple international sites and studies, re-training and evaluating methods on all full available datasets would increase confidence in results. We address the main points below. To preserve anonymity, the GitHub repository is not included in the submission but is already prepared and will be made public after the review process. It contains the full training and inference code, pretrained weights, the exact train/test splits data, and all evaluation scripts used in the paper. 1) Clarification of the anatomical map / site-invariance analysis. We agree that this is a central step and should be described more explicitly. In Ablation Study 2, MMD was computed between every pair of acquisition sites (si ,sj), not between matched subjects. For each site, we pooled the histogram feature vectors from all scans acquired at that site, and computed the RBF-kernel MMD separately for raw-image histograms and anatomical-map histograms. Thus, each value corresponds to one site-pair comparison. The “per-site” summary is the average of that site’s MMD values against all other sites. The paired t-test compares raw vs. anatomical-map MMD on the same site pairs, so the reduction directly reflects lower inter-site discrepancy for the anatomical map. For brevity, we do not reproduce the full pairwise table here. Our anatomical map is intended as a simple low-level prior that suppresses scanner contrast while preserving structure, inspired by recent work on anatomical priors (10.1016/j.neuroimage.2025.121297). Gradient magnitude and high-frequency content are chosen because they are less tied to site-specific intensity statistics than raw signal, and random gamma perturbation further reduces leakage of contrast cues into the conditioning map. 2) Mixed-effects model in Task 1.For each method, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model with site as a fixed effect and subject as a random intercept: tissue_ratio ~ site + (1 | subject) The dependent variable is the GM or WM tissue ratio. These ratios are normalized by total intracranial volume, defined as GM + WM + CSF, to reduce inter-subject size differences and make comparisons across sites and harmonization methods more comparable. 3) Comparison with STGAN / HACA3 and when our method is most useful. We agree that no single method dominates every metric. Our claim is not that diffusion is uniformly best, but that it is the most consistent method in our experiments and provides a strong balance between harmonization and preservation of biologically meaningful signals. In the tissue-level analysis, our method is the only one that consistently achieves both low marginal R² and high conditional R² across GM and WM, whereas STGAN and HACA3 are stronger in one tissue but less consistent in the other. In the cognition analysis, our method achieves the highest global mean absolute correlation and improves over the preprocessed baseline. This is also consistent with Fig. 2, where our method shows fewer over- and under-segmentation errors than the Anatomy Target, suggesting more robust anatomical preservation. At the same time, we acknowledge that STGAN and HACA3 can be stronger in specific metrics or regions. 4) Nature of the contributions / ablations. We appreciate the request for more component-level justification. The manuscript already includes three targeted analyses: guidance ablation (CFG vs. CFG++), the site-invariance test for the anatomical prior, and downstream clinical preservation analyses. Together, these support the full design: patch-based high-resolution synthesis, anatomy-guided conditioning, and manifold-constrained guidance. We also performed an additional internal ablation of the anatomical representation components: removing the gradient component caused a marked SSIM drop (-0.28 drop), indicating that gradient information is the main contributor; removing the high-frequency component did not significantly reduce SSIM, suggesting a smaller contribution. The method introduces anatomy-guided diffusion by constructing site-invariant anatomical maps derived from gradient and high-frequency features. Dear Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs,

We thank you for the careful reading and constructive feedback. We address the main points below.

To preserve anonymity, the GitHub repository is not included in the submission but is already prepared and will be made public after the review process. It contains the full training and inference code, pretrained weights, the exact train/test splits data, and all evaluation scripts used in the paper.

1) Clarification of the anatomical map / site-invariance analysis. We agree that this is a central step and should be described more explicitly. In Ablation Study 2, MMD was computed between every pair of acquisition sites (si ,sj), not between matched subjects. For each site, we pooled the histogram feature vectors from all scans acquired at that site, and computed the RBF-kernel MMD separately for raw-image histograms and anatomical-map histograms. Thus, each value corresponds to one site-pair comparison. The “per-site” summary is the average of that site’s MMD values against all other sites. The paired t-test compares raw vs. anatomical-map MMD on the same site pairs, so the reduction directly reflects lower inter-site discrepancy for the anatomical map. For brevity, we do not reproduce the full pairwise table here. Our anatomical map is intended as a simple low-level prior that suppresses scanner contrast while preserving structure, inspired by recent work on anatomical priors (10.1016/j.neuroimage.2025.121297). Gradient magnitude and high-frequency content are chosen because they are less tied to site-specific intensity statistics than raw signal, and random gamma perturbation further reduces leakage of contrast cues into the conditioning map.

2) Mixed-effects model in Task 1.For each method, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model with site as a fixed effect and subject as a random intercept: tissue_ratio ~ site + (1 | subject) The dependent variable is the GM or WM tissue ratio. These ratios are normalized by total intracranial volume, defined as GM + WM + CSF, to reduce inter-subject size differences and make comparisons across sites and harmonization methods more comparable.

3) Comparison with STGAN / HACA3 and when our method is most useful. We agree that no single method dominates every metric. Our claim is not that diffusion is uniformly best, but that it is the most consistent method in our experiments and provides a strong balance between harmonization and preservation of biologically meaningful signals. In the tissue-level analysis, our method is the only one that consistently achieves both low marginal R² and high conditional R² across GM and WM, whereas STGAN and HACA3 are stronger in one tissue but less consistent in the other. In the cognition analysis, our method achieves the highest global mean absolute correlation and improves over the preprocessed baseline. This is also consistent with Fig. 2, where our method shows fewer over- and under-segmentation errors than the Anatomy Target, suggesting more robust anatomical preservation. At the same time, we acknowledge that STGAN and HACA3 can be stronger in specific metrics or regions.

4) Nature of the contributions / ablations. We appreciate the request for more component-level justification. The manuscript already includes three targeted analyses: guidance ablation (CFG vs. CFG++), the site-invariance test for the anatomical prior, and downstream clinical preservation analyses. Together, these support the full design: patch-based high-resolution synthesis, anatomy-guided conditioning, and manifold-constrained guidance. We also performed an additional internal ablation of the anatomical representation components: removing the gradient component caused a marked SSIM drop (-0.28 drop), indicating that gradient information is the main contributor; removing the high-frequency component did not significantly reduce SSIM, suggesting a smaller contribution. Other components could also merit further investigation.

https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/06.abstract: Zero-shot MRI reconstruction relies on generative priors, but single-modality unconditional priors produce hallucinations under severe ill-posedness. In many clinical workflows, complementary MRI acquisitions (e.g. high-quality structural scans) are routinely available, yet existing reconstruction methods lack mechanisms to leverage this additional information. We propose MPFlow, a zero-shot multi-modal reconstruction framework built on rectified flow that incorporates auxiliary MRI modalities at inference time without retraining the generative prior to improve anatomical fidelity. Cross-modal guidance is enabled by our proposed self-supervised pretraining strategy, Patch-level Multi-modal MR Image Pretraining (PAMRI), which learns shared representations across modalities. Sampling is jointly guided by data consistency and cross-modal feature alignment using pre-trained PAMRI, systematically suppressing intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations. Extensive experiments on HCP and BraTS show that MPFlow matches diffusion baselines on image quality using only 20% of sampling steps while reducing tumor hallucinations by more than 15% (segmentation dice score). This demonstrates that cross-modal guidance enables more reliable and efficient zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Code is available at https://github.com/edshkim98/MPFlow.

  • Please justify your recommendation.

    The authors present an interesting methodology for performing posterior-guided image refinement using an auxiliary image. This wording is specific, as this is not an MRI reconstruction paper, contrary to what the title implies (pointed out by Reviewer 1). However, the authors do define “reconstruction” more broadly as the recreation of high-quality data from limited data. This, however, highlights an issue that is called out in the initial reviews and not addressed. This is the limitation of registered (and seemingly skull-stripped) images in an auxiliary-assisted challenge. This is a strong limitation that is commonly validated in other auxiliary-assisted refinement methods. Further, it takes the method further from the purpose of “reconstruction”, where the assumptions about data preprocessing are necessarily minimal. This is especially true for the two tasks presented here, where registration and skull-stripping would drastically affect the resolution and k-space components.

The reviewers agree that the core idea of inference-time multimodal guidance to reduce hallucination is original and practically motivated, that the PAMRI latent-space alignment is well suited to multi-contrast MRI where pixel-level correspondence is unreliable, and that the evaluation is convincing in going beyond fidelity metrics to include hallucination-related and downstream segmentation measures, all of which are established within the submitted manuscript. https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/07.title: Open World MRI Reconstruction with Bias-Calibrated Adaptation
https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/07.description: Abstract Real-world MRI reconstruction systems face the open-world challenge: test data from unseen imaging centers, anatomical structures, or acquisition protocols can differ drastically from training data, causing severe performance degradation. Existing methods struggle with this challenge. To address this, we propose BiasRecon, a bias-calibrated adaptation framework grounded in the minimal intervention principle: preserve what transfers, calibrate what does not. Concretely, BiasRecon formulates open-world adaptation as an alternating optimization framework that jointly optimizes three components: (1) frequency-guided prior calibration that introduces layer-wise calibration variables to selectively modulate frequency-specific features of the pre-trained score network via self-supervised k-space signals, (2) score-based denoising that leverages the calibrated generative prior for high-fidelity image reconstruction, and (3) adaptive regularization that employs Stein’s Unbiased Risk Estimator to dynamically balance the prior-measurement trade-off, matching test-time noise characteristics without requiring ground truth. By intervening minimally and precisely through this alternating scheme, BiasRecon achieves robust adaptation with fewer than 100 tunable parameters. Extensive experiments across four datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on open-world reconstruction tasks. https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/09.description: Abstract Clinical MRI frequently acquires anisotropic volumes with high in-plane resolution and low through-plane resolution to reduce acquisition time. Multiple orientations are therefore acquired to provide complementary anatomical information. Conventional integration of these views relies on registration followed by interpolation, which can degrade fine structural details. Recent deep learning–based super-resolution (SR) approaches have demonstrated strong performance in enhancing single-view images. However, their clinical reliability is often limited by the need for large-scale training datasets, resulting in increased dependence on cohort-level priors. Self-supervised strategies offer an alternative by learning directly from the target scans. Prior work either neglects the existence of multi-view information or assumes that in-plane information can supervise through-plane reconstruction under the assumption of pre-alignment between images. However, this assumption is rarely satisfied in clinical settings. In this work, we introduce Single-Subject Implicit Multi-View Super-Resolution for MRI (SIMS-MRI), a framework that operates solely on anisotropic multi-view scans from a single patient without requiring pre- or post-processing. Our method combines a multi-resolution hash-encoded implicit representation with learned inter-view alignment to generate a spatially consistent isotropic reconstruction. We validate the SIMS-MRI pipeline on both simulated brain and clinical prostate MRI datasets. The code is publicly available for reproducibility. https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2026/09.abstract: Clinical MRI frequently acquires anisotropic volumes with high in-plane resolution and low through-plane resolution to reduce acquisition time. Multiple orientations are therefore acquired to provide complementary anatomical information. Conventional integration of these views relies on registration followed by interpolation, which can degrade fine structural details. Recent deep learning–based super-resolution (SR) approaches have demonstrated strong performance in enhancing single-view images. However, their clinical reliability is often limited by the need for large-scale training datasets, resulting in increased dependence on cohort-level priors. Self-supervised strategies offer an alternative by learning directly from the target scans. Prior work either neglects the existence of multi-view information or assumes that in-plane information can supervise through-plane reconstruction under the assumption of pre-alignment between images. However, this assumption is rarely satisfied in clinical settings. In this work, we introduce Single-Subject Implicit Multi-View Super-Resolution for MRI (SIMS-MRI), a framework that operates solely on anisotropic multi-view scans from a single patient without requiring pre- or post-processing. Our method combines a multi-resolution hash-encoded implicit representation with learned inter-view alignment to generate a spatially consistent isotropic reconstruction. We validate the SIMS-MRI pipeline on both simulated brain and clinical prostate MRI datasets. The code is publicly available for reproducibility.

    In this paper, the authors propose SIMS-MRI for multi-image super-resolution (MISR) of multiple anisotropic volumes. Their method leverages implicit neural representations (INR) to approximate the image intensities, conduct multi-view registration, and fuse the results into a high-resolution (HR) volume. They accomplish this in three phases. The first phase fits an INR f to the first anisotropic acquisition. The second phase fits an INR g to deformably register the second anisotropic acquisition to the first, using the frozen network f from the first phase. The third phase freezes the registration network g and fine-tunes f to represent both views. During inference, f is queried with isotropic coordinates to yield the estimated HR volume. The authors make use of the InstantNGP feature encoding technique for f and they make use of SIREN for g. To evaluate the efficacy of their method, the authors compare to interpolation and two contemporary single-image super-resolution techniques SMORE and ECLARE in both simulation and real-world experiments. The authors report superior performance across several quantitative metrics compared to the other methods across all experiments.

Non-linear deformation might be helpful for prostate MRI due to possible bowel movement which is non-linear, but most of the time affine transformation (12 DOF) is sufficient. Why not just directly learn the 12 affine transformation parameters rather than using an INR to parametrize a dense displacement field which is close to affine anyway due to the strong bending energy constraint? Using INR for an underlying transformation that is near-affine offers marginal benefit and is an overkill. 1.c. Consider reporting what \alpha for the bending energy regularization is used for the in vivo clinical prostate MRI experiment. 2.Additional experiments would be helpful for the readers to better appreciate the work. 2.a. For example, it would be helpful to see a visualization (if space permits) of the results in Table 2.It would be interesting to see what w/o FreeNeRF & w/ HE looks like since it gives slightly worse performance according to conventional metrics but slightly better performance according to learning-based metrics. 2.b. In might be helpful to also report runtime/number of parameters in Table 1 since the authors intend this work to eventually have clinical applications where speed is important. 2.c. Table 1 only reports result on a single simulated data. Consider randomly choosing a couple of (say, 10) different rotation angles and report metrics over these 10 experiments. The rationale for this suggestion is that there is no other result in the paper that test for the robustness of Phase 2: Implicit Image Registration. 3.Regarding the in vivo prostate MRI experiment. 3.a. The authors are aware of the lack of ground truth for in vivo prostate MRI experiment. However, it makes little sense to compare reconstructed slices to the closest slice in the “ground truth” just to avoid blurring introduced by registration. Doing so makes Fig. 3 very hard to interpret. 3.b. In Fig. 3, only perceptual metric from MONAI is reported. It doesn’t hurt to also report other metrics, e.g., MAE, PSNR, SSIM, along with the learning-based metrics, as long as the authors provide explanations of why some of these metrics do not necessarily reflect true visual quality of the reconstruction.

    There are some typographical errors, e.g., spaces in front of citations.

• Please describe the contribution of the paper

    The paper introduces SIMS-MRI, a single-subject INR for multi-view super resolution. The paper proposes a 3-stage pipeline to train INRs, register multiview signals, and learn a fused multiview signal representation for isotropic and potentially high-resolution volume reconstruction. Overall, the work provides a stable and good setup for approaching such problems.

Please provide details, for instance, if a method is novel, explain what aspect is novel and why this is interesting.

    1.Decoupling the INR training and registration step seems like a good way to handle misaligned data. Furthermore, INRs excel at showing generalizability with homogeneous data – which makes the decoupled registration even more interesting. 2.Qualitative results show that SIMS-MRI has substantial improvements over prior methods. Quantitative results further confirm its performance. A real-world clinical example also shows that SIMS-MRI captures high-frequency details better than prior methods; however, it seems to lack contrast.

    1.The paper sets up the problem that MRIs have poor through-plane resolution, and then goes on to propose a multiview interpolation scheme, mainly using INRs. Results, however, do not show an improvement or explicit evaluation on through-plane MRI slices – demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method, particularly with respect to the problem stated in its introduction. 2.It is unclear whether the simulation has realistic in-plane and through-plane sampling rates, and whether the evaluation for interpolation performance is happening on unsampled slices. 3.Can the authors comment on how their model performs when the in-plane: through-plane sampling ratio changes? We thank R1, R2, R3, and Rmeta for their constructive feedback and encouraging comments. All suggestions, including minor writing improvements, will be reflected in the camera-ready version as rules and space permit. We address the remaining concerns below.

Novelty (Rmeta and R2): We agree on shared similarities with NeSVOR and IREM. However, NeSVOR addresses only rigid motion, and IREM requires pre-registered volumes. SIMS-MRI incorporates its own registration step, eliminating prior alignment while handling linear/nonlinear misalignment, making it more generalizable for clinical MR settings where anisotropic acquisitions are the norm. We will cite both and clarify.

Slice thickness, spacing, and simulation (R1, R3 and Rmeta): For brain, we 4× downsampled isotropic images (e.g., 1×1×1 mm → 1×1×4 mm); for prostate, native slice thickness is 3 mm (Sec. 3.2). Anisotropic volumes are used as-is (no further subsampling) by converting directly to intensity point sets. The final isotropic inference grid uses the original GT grid for brain and a 1×1×1 mm subsampled grid for prostate. We acknowledge that modeling the physical slice-selection profile and through-plane PSF for simulation would produce a more realistic simulation. We see this as future work. Importantly, evaluation always uses the held-out sagittal view unseen during training, testing recovery of an unseen orientation.

Runtime and parameters (R1, R2 and Rmeta): End-to-end processing could take as little as 20 min/subject on a single A100.Implementation is unoptimized. Multi-GPU support and better implementation could substantially reduce this. Parameter counts (hash encoder (268.4M), MLP (4.7M), and registration model (0.1M)) will be reported in the camera-ready.

Pseudo-GT and metrics for prostate (R1, R2): We are aware of the pseudo-GT limitation and will discuss it explicitly in camera-ready. Following R1’s suggestion, we simulated 3 mm thick slices via rect and Gaussian convolution. Results were consistent with reported findings. On MAE/PSNR/SSIM, rankings are mixed across methods. In addition to misregistration, these metrics are sensitive to contrast changes, which might explain the mixed results. DISTS and MONAI metrics show SIMS-MRI significantly outperforming baselines.

NCC vs MSE; non-linear deformation; bending energy α (R2): We chose NCC because MRI intensity profiles can shift across acquisitions, making MSE unreliable. Results with MSE had misalignments in neck/facial regions. For deformation, we began with 12-parameter affine registration for brain (yielding similar results), but adopted non-linear deformation to maintain a general-purpose architecture suitable for all experiments and to handle misalignments in non-brain area. For prostate, we used no regularizer (α=0). These settings are application-specific and will be noted as a tunable choice in the discussion.

Additional experiments (FreeNeRF/HE visualization; additional simulation scenario) (R2): Both sets of experiments are complete. We tested randomly chosen rotation+translation combinations for brain, with results close to those reported. We will include these and the visualizations as rules permit.

Additional view for better SR (R2): Great point. As follow-up work, we are working on a method to utilize all available series (views, contrasts, etc) in a study. We will mention this as future work.

Through-plane clarification; anisotropy ratio study (R3): The paper reports results on through-plane slices: only LR axial and coronal views were used for training, and performance is evaluated on the held-out sagittal GT. We will revise the text to clarify. Regarding varying in-plane: through-plane ratios, conceptually, SIMS-MRI benefits most when orthogonal views provide complementary high-resolution in-plane information, and should degrade as anisotropy increases or view complementarity decreases. A systematic anisotropy ratio study is an important direction we will include in future work.

    This paper received mixed reviews that should be addressed in a rebuttal. The split among the reviewers is mainly about novelty and problem formulation rather than whether the method works. The paper addresses a meaningful MRI SR setting from multiple anisotropic acquisitions using only the anisotropic image. The reviewers found the decoupled INR registration and reconstruction setup promising and the results convincing with extensive analysis. However, there are substantial concerns about the novelty of the approach, especially with regards to NeSVoR. The rebuttal should focus on this aspect. There are other, more minor, concerns that should be addressed such as the forward model definition, clarification between sparse slices and thick slices, and runtime.

  • Please justify your recommendation.

    This paper maintains mixed reviews after rebuttal, but the authors have provided clear and detailed explanations that address the majority of the reviewers’ concerns. Novelty remains a concern, but the motivation for the methodology is quite clear and supported by clinical and physical reality. I would argue that non-rigid motion can be accepted between modalities, especially outside of the brain, and should be considered a known quantity. However, this should be directly evaluated at a later time. The author’s rationale for using NCC is frequently cited in MRI registration literature. Given the authors’ rebuttal and their addressing of the concerns, I will recommend acceptance for this paper.

    After rebuttal, I recommend Accept. The authors addressed many key technical and presentation concerns, including slice thickness/anisotropic spacing, held-out sagittal evaluation, prostate pseudo-GT limitations, runtime/parameter counts, and the rationale for NCC and nonlinear registration. They also added requested experiments on realistic slice-profile simulation and additional motion settings. Some weaknesses remain, particularly regarding comparison with NeSVoR/IREM. However, the paper presents a useful single-subject multi-view MRI super-resolution framework that integrates registration and fusion without large supervised datasets. Given the positive critiques from R1 and R3, improved clarity after rebuttal, and clinical relevance, I recommend acceptance.

Although the novelty is somewhat incremental and the physical slice-profile modeling could be stronger, the method is technically sound, experimentally convincing, and useful for the community, so I recommend acceptance.
